rituals.name: DISASTER TRAILER CUT
rituals.title: DISASTER TRAILER CUT
rituals.targetPattern: Cinematic amplification of threat
rituals.target_pattern: Cinematic amplification of threat
rituals.precise_subpattern: Cinematic amplification of threat
rituals.vibeLine: Your brain added thunder, slow motion and a villain soundtrack. Cute.
rituals.hook: Give the worry the movie trailer it has clearly been auditioning for.
rituals.predict: Guess which version will feel more dangerous: the dramatic trailer or the boring CCTV cut.
rituals.play: Describe the feared situation for 10 sec like a blockbuster trailer. Replay the exact same event like silent CCTV: who, where, what movement, what words.
rituals.catch: Check if the body reacts differently even though the basic event stayed the same.
rituals.reveal: Editing changed the emotional impact before reality changed at all.
rituals.mindBend: The problem may be real. The director’s cut in your head is optional.

rituals.vibeLine: Turns out your single camera angle was not the entire Netflix production.
rituals.hook: You have one camera angle and your brain has already written everyone else’s dialogue.
rituals.predict: Guess how many plausible explanations you can create without changing the visible facts.
rituals.play: Picture the situation from three impossible camera positions: behind the other person, five minutes before, and five minutes after. Give each angle one plausible detail you did not see.
rituals.catch: Notice how easily the meaning changes when hidden context changes.
rituals.reveal: The original interpretation was one camera angle, not the whole set.
rituals.mindBend: What you cannot see is exactly where certainty likes to invent furniture.

unfiltered.catch: Notice how easily the meaning changes when hidden context changes.
unfiltered.reveal: The original interpretation was one camera angle, not the whole set.
unfiltered.mindBend: What you cannot see is exactly where certainty likes to invent furniture.
unfiltered.safety:
PAUSE
Use the mental image to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.
unfiltered.targetPattern: Filling unseen social information
unfiltered.theoryBackbone: Attribution theory; ambiguity; perspective taking
unfiltered.mechanismFingerprint: Generate counterfactual unseen viewpoints to demonstrate underdetermination of social interpretations.

rituals.name: PREDICTION TIMESTAMP
rituals.title: PREDICTION TIMESTAMP
rituals.targetPattern: Future statements treated as current facts
rituals.target_pattern: Future statements treated as current facts
rituals.precise_subpattern: Future statements treated as current facts
rituals.vibeLine: Amazing what one timestamp does to a fake breaking-news alert.
rituals.hook: Your future thought arrived without a date stamp.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the sentence feels different after you attach the exact future time it claims to know.
rituals.play: Add a timestamp to the prediction: “At 3:20 pm tomorrow, I predict…” Say the whole sentence again with the timestamp.
rituals.catch: Check if it sounds more like a forecast and less like a fact happening now.
rituals.reveal: Time-stamping forces a prediction back into the future where it belongs.
rituals.mindBend: A forecast is not evidence from the future. It is a guess made in the present.

rituals.precise_subpattern: Searching only for one interpretation
rituals.vibeLine: Your favourite theory just discovered it has competition.

rituals.predict: Guess how hard it will be to argue the opposite explanation using the same facts.

rituals.catch: Check if the “impossible” opposite becomes surprisingly easy to defend.
rituals.reveal: If the same evidence can support two stories, the evidence did not uniquely prove the first one.
rituals.mindBend: Your first explanation may be convincing without being exclusive.

One bad chapter does not automatically get a plural.

rituals.targetPattern: Blending observation, memory and fear
rituals.target_pattern: Blending observation, memory and fear
rituals.precise_subpattern: Blending observation, memory and fear
rituals.vibeLine: Turns out “I know” had a lot of “I guessed” hiding inside.
rituals.hook: Let’s label the ingredients before your brain serves them as one soup.
rituals.predict: Guess which source is doing most of the work: saw, heard, remembered, guessed, or feared.
rituals.play: Break the thought into short chunks and tag each chunk with one source word: SAW, HEARD, REMEMBERED, GUESSED, FEARED.
rituals.catch: Look for the moment a guess or fear started sounding like something you saw.
rituals.reveal: Different mental sources can feel equally vivid while having very different evidential status.
rituals.mindBend: Vivid is a volume setting, not a source certificate.

rituals.name: HEADLINE VS TRANSCRIPT
rituals.title: HEADLINE VS TRANSCRIPT
rituals.targetPattern: Headlines compressing nuance into verdicts
rituals.target_pattern: Headlines compressing nuance into verdicts
rituals.precise_subpattern: Headlines compressing nuance into verdicts
rituals.vibeLine: Your brain runs a tabloid. The transcript is less dramatic.
rituals.hook: Your brain wrote a headline.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the headline sounds harsher than a word-for-word transcript.
rituals.play: Write the thought as a six-word headline. Under it, write the plain transcript of what happened, including pauses and boring details.
rituals.catch: Compare what the headline deleted to make the story punchier.
rituals.reveal: Compression removes context, and the missing context is often where nuance lived.
rituals.mindBend: A headline can be accurate enough to sting and incomplete enough to mislead.

rituals.name: COUNTEREXAMPLE FLASH

rituals.targetPattern: Ignoring disconfirming instances
rituals.target_pattern: Ignoring disconfirming instances
rituals.precise_subpattern: Ignoring disconfirming instances
rituals.vibeLine: One annoying little fact just broke your brain’s sweeping statement.
rituals.hook: One tiny exception can ruin a very bossy rule.
rituals.predict: Guess how quickly you can find a real example that does not fit the belief perfectly.
rituals.play: If the thought says “I always fail,” find one thing you completed. If it says “nobody likes me,” find one neutral or warm interaction. You need only one honest exception.
rituals.catch: Check if the absolute sentence now needs editing.
rituals.reveal: Counterexamples do not prove the opposite. They simply stop an absolute from pretending it has no exceptions.
rituals.mindBend: You do not need a positive lie. One honest exception is enough to break an absolute.

rituals.name: SUBTITLES OFF
rituals.title: SUBTITLES OFF
rituals.targetPattern: Invented internal dialogue of others
rituals.target_pattern: Invented internal dialogue of others
rituals.precise_subpattern: Invented internal dialogue of others
rituals.vibeLine: Your brain added closed captions to a face.
rituals.hook: Mute the subtitles you secretly added to someone else’s face.
rituals.predict: Guess how much of the thought disappears if you are not allowed to write their internal dialogue.
rituals.play: Replay the scene with one rule: no sentences beginning “they think,” “they must,” “they probably,” or “they meant.” Keep only visible behaviour and spoken words.
rituals.catch: Notice the blank spaces where the imaginary subtitles used to be.
rituals.reveal: Silence in another person’s mind is uncomfortable, so your brain often fills it fast.
rituals.mindBend: No subtitle appeared above their head. Your brain added one in post-production.

rituals.vibeLine: Your “obvious” conclusion brought a whole entourage.

rituals.predict: Guess how many separate things must be true before your conclusion can be true.
rituals.play: Say the conclusion. Keep asking, “What has to be true for that?” Write each answer as a separate domino until you reach something directly observed.
rituals.catch: Count how many unverified dominoes sit between the observation and the conclusion.
rituals.reveal: The conclusion felt like one thought, but it may depend on a whole chain of guesses.
rituals.mindBend: Certainty often hides inside compression: five assumptions can arrive wearing one sentence.

rituals.name: TRAIT OR TRAFFIC?
rituals.title: TRAIT OR TRAFFIC?
rituals.targetPattern: Treating behaviour as personality while ignoring situation
rituals.target_pattern: Treating behaviour as personality while ignoring situation
rituals.precise_subpattern: Treating behaviour as personality while ignoring situation
rituals.vibeLine: One weird moment and your brain already printed business cards.
rituals.hook: Did they reveal their personality—or did you catch them in weather?
rituals.predict: Guess whether your explanation changes when the exact behaviour is done by someone you already like.
rituals.play: Take the behaviour you’re judging. First finish: “They did that because they are ___.” Then finish: “They did that because the situation was ___.” Use the same event.
rituals.catch: Notice which version felt automatic and which one required imagination.
rituals.reveal: Person explanations arrive faster than situation explanations, especially when we’re annoyed.
rituals.mindBend: A behaviour can be evidence about a moment without being a biography of a person.

rituals.name: WHAT COUNTS AS FAILURE?
rituals.title: WHAT COUNTS AS FAILURE?
rituals.targetPattern: A vague negative label with moving criteria
rituals.target_pattern: A vague negative label with moving criteria
rituals.precise_subpattern: A vague negative label with moving criteria
rituals.vibeLine: Your label was powerful right up until it needed terms and conditions.
rituals.hook: Let’s make your scary label pass a definition test.
rituals.predict: Guess whether your current event still qualifies as “failure” under a rule you would apply consistently.
rituals.play: Write 1 line beginning, “For anything to count as failure, it must…” Make the rule concrete enough to use on someone else. Now test today’s event against it.
rituals.catch: Watch whether the label survives once its criteria stop moving around your mood.
rituals.reveal: Vague labels can win arguments because they never have to meet a fixed threshold.
rituals.mindBend: A verdict with no stable definition can convict almost anything.

rituals.name: RED DOT ON WHITE PAPER
rituals.title: RED DOT ON WHITE PAPER
rituals.targetPattern: One negative item dominating mixed evidence
rituals.target_pattern: One negative item dominating mixed evidence
rituals.precise_subpattern: One negative item dominating mixed evidence
rituals.vibeLine: Your brain found the one red pixel and wrote a review.
rituals.hook: Your attention found the red dot.
rituals.predict: Imagine a white page with one red dot. Guess which part your eyes would report first.
rituals.play: Now map the current situation the same way: name the one negative detail your mind keeps circling, then name three neutral or positive details that are also on the page.
rituals.catch: Check if the red detail became less true—or simply less alone.
rituals.reveal: Threat-relevant details are designed to win attention, not to provide a balanced summary.
rituals.mindBend: What grabs attention can be important without being proportionate.

rituals.name: EXPIRY DATE ON PROOF
rituals.title: EXPIRY DATE ON PROOF
rituals.targetPattern: Old evidence treated as permanently current
rituals.target_pattern: Old evidence treated as permanently current
rituals.precise_subpattern: Old evidence treated as permanently current
rituals.vibeLine: That belief is running on legacy software.
rituals.hook: Some evidence is still valid.
rituals.predict: Pick the strongest evidence behind the belief. Guess how old it is.
rituals.play: For each piece of evidence, add a date or era: today, this month, last year, childhood, unknown. Ask: “What newer information has arrived since?”
rituals.catch: Check if the belief is being powered by data from a different version of the situation—or of you.
rituals.reveal: Evidence can remain relevant while losing freshness.
rituals.mindBend: Old evidence deserves context, not eternal tenure.

rituals.name: FAKE CHIP TEST
rituals.title: FAKE CHIP TEST
rituals.targetPattern: Confidence untested against consequences
rituals.target_pattern: Confidence untested against consequences
rituals.precise_subpattern: Confidence untested against consequences
rituals.vibeLine: Ninety percent certain… but suddenly very protective of one fake point?
rituals.hook: No money. One imaginary point. Would you still bet on the thought?
rituals.predict: Rate confidence first: 0–100.
rituals.play: Now imagine you gain one point if the prediction is right and lose one if it is wrong. Choose: BET or PASS. Don’t justify it.
rituals.catch: Compare your confidence number with your willingness to risk even one meaningless point.
rituals.reveal: When a belief has to guide a choice, confidence often becomes more honest.
rituals.mindBend: A number can perform confidence. A choice has to use it.

rituals.target_pattern: Judging a decision only by what happened later

rituals.vibeLine: Easy to be a genius after the credits roll.
rituals.hook: Let’s judge the decision using only information that existed when you made it.
rituals.predict: Guess whether you would criticise the choice as harshly if the ending were hidden.

rituals.name: POSSIBLE IS A HUGE COUNTRY
rituals.title: POSSIBLE IS A HUGE COUNTRY
rituals.targetPattern: Possible treated as imminent
rituals.target_pattern: Possible treated as imminent
rituals.precise_subpattern: Possible treated as imminent
rituals.vibeLine: Your brain moved into POSSIBLE and started acting like it was EXPECTED.
rituals.hook: “Possible” covers everything from meteor strike to missed bus.
rituals.predict: Ask: is your worry merely possible, reasonably plausible, or expected soon?
rituals.play: Draw three imaginary boxes: POSSIBLE, PLAUSIBLE, EXPECTED. Put the feared event in one box based on the evidence you have—not on how unpleasant it would be.
rituals.catch: Check if your body had been reacting to the first box as though it were the third.
rituals.reveal: Possibility answers “can it happen?” It does not answer “how much should I expect it?”
rituals.mindBend: Possible is not a probability. It is a very large country.
rituals.ritualCard:
“Possible” covers everything from meteor strike to missed bus.
Draw three imaginary boxes: POSSIBLE, PLAUSIBLE, EXPECTED. Put the feared event in one box based on the evidence you have—not on how unpleasant it would be.
Ask: is your worry merely possible, reasonably plausible, or expected soon?
Check if your body had been reacting to the first box as though it were the third. Possibility answers “can it happen?” It does not answer “how much should I expect it?”
↻ POSSIBLE IS A HUGE COUNTRY

rituals.name: ONE RED MARBLE
rituals.title: ONE RED MARBLE
rituals.targetPattern: One bad case obscuring the full sample
rituals.target_pattern: One bad case obscuring the full sample
rituals.precise_subpattern: One bad case obscuring the full sample
rituals.vibeLine: One red marble was doing a suspicious amount of PR.
rituals.hook: Your brain found the red marble.
rituals.predict: Guess what percentage of the whole sample the bad example actually represents.
rituals.play: Imagine ten marbles for the last ten relevant events. Colour only the genuinely bad ones red; leave the rest another colour.
rituals.catch: Look at the ratio, not the emotional brightness of the reddest marble.
rituals.reveal: A vivid negative can dominate attention while occupying a small denominator.
rituals.mindBend: One red marble can feel like the whole bag when the bag disappears.

rituals.vibeLine: Interesting. The scary word was hiding a much smaller number.

rituals.name: THE TWIN TIMELINE
rituals.title: THE TWIN TIMELINE
rituals.targetPattern: Outcome blamed on one choice despite many possible worlds
rituals.target_pattern: Outcome blamed on one choice despite many possible worlds
rituals.precise_subpattern: Outcome blamed on one choice despite many possible worlds
rituals.vibeLine: Your imaginary timeline was suspiciously convenient.
rituals.hook: Your brain picked one alternate universe and called it evidence.
rituals.predict: Guess how many different outcomes could follow the opposite choice.
rituals.play: Imagine a twin-you made the opposite decision. Give that twin three plausible endings: better, similar, and worse.
rituals.catch: Check if your original “if only” had quietly assumed just one ending.
rituals.reveal: Counterfactuals feel factual because we can picture them, not because we observed them.
rituals.mindBend: The road not taken is not a recorded documentary.

rituals.title: CROWD WITHOUT FACES
rituals.targetPattern: Assuming others share the same standard or reaction
rituals.target_pattern: Assuming others share the same standard or reaction
rituals.precise_subpattern: Assuming others share the same standard or reaction
rituals.vibeLine: Unanimous jury cancelled due to actual humans being different.
rituals.hook: Your brain invented a unanimous audience.
rituals.predict: Guess how many out of ten reasonable people would actually react the same way.
rituals.play: Picture ten faceless people with different ages, moods and priorities. Assign three possible reactions across them instead of one unanimous verdict.
rituals.catch: Notice how quickly certainty drops when the imaginary crowd gains diversity.
rituals.reveal: We often project our own standard onto a crowd that does not exist.
rituals.mindBend: An imagined audience is easiest to fear when everyone in it has the same face.

rituals.target_pattern: Visible successes hiding invisible attempts
rituals.precise_subpattern: Visible successes hiding invisible attempts
rituals.vibeLine: The highlight reel forgot to include the bin folder.
rituals.hook: You are comparing yourself with survivors, not the full audition list.
rituals.predict: Guess how many unseen attempts might sit behind the visible success.
rituals.play: Take one success that intimidates you. Add an imaginary backstage row for failed drafts, ignored posts, rejected tries, boring repetitions and luck.
rituals.catch: Notice how the visible outcome changes once invisible attempts are allowed back in.
rituals.reveal: Success stories are easy to see; non-surviving attempts rarely advertise themselves.
rituals.mindBend: Visible winners are not the same thing as visible odds.

rituals.vibeLine: Your thought has airtime, not necessarily proof.
rituals.hook: You have heard that thought a lot.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the belief feels true partly because it is familiar.
rituals.play: Say the belief once. Ask: “What new evidence did repetition add?” If the answer is none, write REPEATED, NOT VERIFIED.
rituals.catch: Notice how repetition and evidence separate.
rituals.reveal: Familiar statements become easier to process, and ease can feel like truth.
rituals.mindBend: A sentence can become comfortable in your head without becoming correct.

rituals.name: MIDDLE OF THE MOVIE
rituals.title: MIDDLE OF THE MOVIE
rituals.targetPattern: A whole event judged by its worst moment and ending
rituals.target_pattern: A whole event judged by its worst moment and ending
rituals.precise_subpattern: A whole event judged by its worst moment and ending
rituals.vibeLine: Your worst five minutes became press secretary for the whole day.
rituals.hook: Your memory kept the peak and the ending.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the event was awful every minute or mainly at a few points.
rituals.play: Divide the event into beginning, middle, peak, end. Give each a 0–10 rating instead of one overall score.
rituals.catch: Compare the average shape with the remembered verdict.
rituals.reveal: Memory often overweights peaks and endings when summarising experiences.
rituals.mindBend: The worst minute can become the spokesperson for an entire hour.

rituals.vibeLine: Your brain wrote fan fiction after the evidence ended.
rituals.hook: Your brain finished a sentence reality never wrote.
rituals.predict: Guess the exact ending your mind supplied after the last known fact.
rituals.play: State only what is known, then stop mid-story at that point. Put every later conclusion in brackets labelled [UNSEEN].
rituals.catch: Notice how much distress lives after the factual sentence ends.
rituals.reveal: The mind hates blanks and often fills them with its favourite threat.
rituals.mindBend: A missing ending is uncertainty, not permission to print the worst one.

VIBE: UNFILTERED

A spike is not automatically the new damn normal.

HOOK
Extreme moments feel like new permanent settings.

PREDICT
Guess whether the next reading, mood, performance or reaction will be equally extreme.

PLAY
Think of three previous unusually high or low moments in any ordinary area. Ask what happened on the next measurement or day.

CATCH
Notice how often extremes drifted back toward ordinary ranges.

REVEAL
Extreme observations naturally have more room to move toward typical levels.

MIND BEND
An extreme moment can be real without becoming the new baseline.

MOVE ON
↻ EXTREME DOESN’T SETTLE THERE

rituals.name: MOVE THE RULER
rituals.title: MOVE THE RULER
rituals.targetPattern: An outcome judged against an arbitrary comparison point
rituals.target_pattern: An outcome judged against an arbitrary comparison point
rituals.precise_subpattern: An outcome judged against an arbitrary comparison point
rituals.vibeLine: Your expectation brought its own grading curve.
rituals.hook: The result did not change.
rituals.predict: Guess how you would feel if you had expected half as much—or twice as much.
rituals.play: Hold the actual outcome fixed. Compare it against three reference points: low expectation, realistic expectation, inflated expectation.
rituals.catch: Notice how disappointment or success changes while the outcome stays identical.
rituals.reveal: Evaluation depends partly on the reference point chosen.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes the pain is not only the result. It is the ruler you placed beside it.

rituals.name: THE MISSING DENOMINATOR
rituals.title: THE MISSING DENOMINATOR
rituals.targetPattern: A small count feeling huge because the total pool is ignored

rituals.vibeLine: Three sounds scary. Three out of forty has different shoes.
rituals.hook: Three bad moments sounds enormous until we ask: three out of how many?
rituals.predict: Guess the total number of comparable moments in the same period.

rituals.reveal: Counts feel bigger when the background population is invisible.
rituals.mindBend: A number without its denominator is wearing platform shoes.

rituals.name: EXTREME DAY, BORING AVERAGE
rituals.title: EXTREME DAY, BORING AVERAGE
rituals.targetPattern: A temporary extreme treated as a permanent direction
rituals.target_pattern: A temporary extreme treated as a permanent direction
rituals.precise_subpattern: A temporary extreme treated as a permanent direction
rituals.vibeLine: One wild Tuesday is not a trend line.
rituals.hook: Your worst day applied to become your permanent trend line.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the next few similar days are likely to be equally extreme, worse, or closer to normal.
rituals.play: Pick one unusually bad or unusually good recent day. Now list three more ordinary examples from the same area before or after it.
rituals.catch: Compare the extreme point with the little cluster around it.
rituals.reveal: Extreme observations are often followed by less extreme ones even when nobody fixes anything.
rituals.mindBend: An outlier can be real without becoming a direction.

rituals.target_pattern: A preselected option feeling like the correct one
rituals.precise_subpattern: A preselected option feeling like the correct one
rituals.vibeLine: The default was acting very confident for a checkbox.
rituals.hook: Sometimes the easiest option feels right because someone else pre-ticked the box.
rituals.predict: Guess whether you would choose the same thing if every option began equally blank.
rituals.play: Take the choice in front of you. Imagine none of the options is current, normal, expected, or preselected. Which one would you choose from a clean screen?
rituals.catch: Check if the current option loses authority when its default status disappears.
rituals.reveal: Defaults guide behaviour even when they contain no special evidence.
rituals.mindBend: Familiar is a setting, not a verdict.

rituals.target_pattern: Equivalent outcomes feeling different under gain versus loss wording
rituals.precise_subpattern: Equivalent outcomes feeling different under gain versus loss wording
rituals.vibeLine: The maths did not move. Your mood apparently did.
rituals.hook: Let’s see whether the wording can push the same number around.
rituals.predict: Guess which feels better: “keep 80%” or “lose 20%.”
rituals.play: Apply both frames to your own issue using the same underlying quantity. Say the gain frame once, then the loss frame once.
rituals.catch: Check if your emotional reaction changes while the arithmetic stays fixed.
rituals.reveal: Equivalent facts can produce different reactions when the frame changes.
rituals.mindBend: If the maths stayed still but the feeling moved, the label was doing work.

rituals.name: SCALE IT TENFOLD
rituals.title: SCALE IT TENFOLD
rituals.targetPattern: Emotional response not scaling with actual size
rituals.target_pattern: Emotional response not scaling with actual size
rituals.precise_subpattern: Emotional response not scaling with actual size
rituals.vibeLine: Apparently “bad” was doing more work than the number.
rituals.hook: Your reaction may be responding to the category, not the amount.
rituals.predict: Guess whether the feeling changes proportionally when the quantity changes by ten times.
rituals.play: Take the feared quantity. Imagine it at one-tenth the size, then ten times the size. Compare your emotional response to each version.
rituals.catch: Check if the feeling barely moves even when the scale does.
rituals.reveal: Emotions often respond to “bad thing” as a category before they respond accurately to magnitude.
rituals.mindBend: If ten times the amount creates nearly the same feeling, your alarm may be reading labels more than scale.

rituals.targetPattern: Previous outcomes treated as changing independent odds
rituals.target_pattern: Previous outcomes treated as changing independent odds

rituals.vibeLine: Apparently heads did not leave a debt note for tails.
rituals.hook: The last five outcomes are staring at the next one like they have influence.
rituals.predict: Guess whether five heads makes tails more likely on the next fair toss.
rituals.play: Picture a fair coin landing heads five times. Before toss six, erase the first five tosses from the table. Ask what physically changed inside the coin.
rituals.catch: Check if the feeling of 'tails is due' survives the empty table.
rituals.reveal: Independent events do not repay imbalance on schedule.
rituals.mindBend: The universe does not owe your streak a correction.

rituals.targetPattern: Limited availability inflating perceived value
rituals.target_pattern: Limited availability inflating perceived value
rituals.precise_subpattern: Limited availability inflating perceived value
rituals.vibeLine: One left! Same object. More adrenaline.
rituals.hook: The words 'only one left' added emotional glitter.
rituals.predict: Guess how much you would want the same thing if there were fifty available.
rituals.play: Take the scarce option. Imagine the stock counter changes from 1 left to 50 available with everything else identical.
rituals.catch: Notice what happens to urgency and desirability.
rituals.reveal: Scarcity can increase perceived value without improving the thing itself.
rituals.mindBend: Running out is information about supply, not automatically about fit.

Take one uncertain outcome. Write two boxes: KNOWN BAD and UNKNOWN. Ask what actual evidence says the unknown belongs above, below, or equal to the known risk.
Guess whether 'unknown chance' feels worse than a known 30% chance even without evidence.
Notice if uncertainty itself was being charged as extra danger. Ambiguity feels aversive because missing information is uncomfortable.
↻ UNKNOWN IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY WORSE

rituals.name: ONE CAUSE IS TOO TIDY
rituals.title: ONE CAUSE IS TOO TIDY
rituals.targetPattern: One neat explanation crowding out multiple contributing causes
rituals.target_pattern: One neat explanation crowding out multiple contributing causes
rituals.precise_subpattern: One neat explanation crowding out multiple contributing causes
rituals.vibeLine: Three boring contributors just ruined the conspiracy.
rituals.hook: Real life is usually messier than one villain.
rituals.predict: Guess how many different small causes could contribute to the same outcome.
rituals.play: Take the event. Ban yourself from using one master explanation. Name three contributors from different categories: person, timing, environment, chance, system, history.
rituals.catch: Check if the story becomes less satisfying and more realistic.
rituals.reveal: Human outcomes are often multiply determined.
rituals.mindBend: A neat cause can be emotionally satisfying precisely because reality is untidy.

rituals.mindBend: A conclusion does not inherit eternal life from its first proof.

rituals.vibeLine: Very reasonable-looking choice. Conveniently surrounded by chaos.

rituals.targetPattern: How categories are divided changing perceived importance
rituals.target_pattern: How categories are divided changing perceived importance
rituals.precise_subpattern: How categories are divided changing perceived importance
rituals.vibeLine: Apparently getting your own category is a power move.
rituals.hook: Your categories may be secretly voting.
rituals.predict: Guess which life area looks biggest depending on how finely you split it.
rituals.play: Take one issue and divide it two ways. Example: WORK vs LIFE, then WORK / FAMILY / HEALTH / FRIENDS / REST / FUN. Compare where attention seems to go.
rituals.catch: Notice how the partition itself changes what feels prominent.
rituals.reveal: What gets its own box often receives extra psychological weight.
rituals.mindBend: Categories do not merely describe attention; they can allocate it.

rituals.vibeLine: One sure thing came with a very large ego.

rituals.reveal: Partial certainty can dominate choice beyond its actual contribution.
rituals.mindBend: A guaranteed corner is still only a corner.

rituals.targetPattern: One presented unit feeling like the correct amount
rituals.target_pattern: One presented unit feeling like the correct amount
rituals.precise_subpattern: One presented unit feeling like the correct amount
rituals.vibeLine: One portion is just a designer's opinion with edges.
rituals.hook: Your brain loves finishing whatever arrived as 'one.'
rituals.predict: Guess whether the same amount feels different when packaged as one big unit versus two small ones.
rituals.play: Imagine the same snack, task, budget, or time block divided into one unit, two units, or four. Which amount suddenly feels 'normal'?
rituals.catch: Notice how packaging can create an invisible stopping rule.
rituals.reveal: Presented units become behavioural defaults.
rituals.mindBend: One unit is a suggestion disguised as a natural amount.

rituals.hook: Remove the impressive title and see what the sentence can do alone.

rituals.title: FEELING ISN'T A RISK CALCULATOR

rituals.precise_subpattern: Good/bad feeling standing in for separate risk and benefit judgments
rituals.vibeLine: You can love the thing and still price the downside.
rituals.hook: If you like something, your brain may quietly lower its risks too.
rituals.predict: Guess how your risk estimate changes when you imagine liking versus disliking the same option.
rituals.play: Take one choice. Rate BENEFIT and RISK separately before writing whether you personally like it.
rituals.catch: Check if the two numbers had been moving together simply because your feeling was global.
rituals.reveal: Overall affect can substitute for separate analysis of costs and benefits.
rituals.mindBend: Liking something does not make its risks smaller.

VIBE: CHEEKY

One crisp number was doing a lot of confidence theatre.

HOOK
Your estimate came with suspiciously skinny uncertainty.

PREDICT
Guess the lowest and highest value you would not be shocked to see.

PLAY
Take your single estimate—time, cost, probability, score. Replace it with a range: low / best guess / high.

CATCH
Notice how much certainty was hiding inside one neat number.

REVEAL
Point estimates conceal uncertainty that ranges make visible.

MIND BEND
Precision can look like knowledge even when it is just formatting.

MOVE ON
↻ WIDEN THE ERROR BARS

rituals.name: PRIVATE WEIRDNESS CLUB
rituals.title: PRIVATE WEIRDNESS CLUB
rituals.targetPattern: Assuming one's awkward reaction is rarer than it is
rituals.target_pattern: Assuming one's awkward reaction is rarer than it is
rituals.precise_subpattern: Assuming one's awkward reaction is rarer than it is
rituals.vibeLine: Plot twist: humans are embarrassingly human.
rituals.hook: Your embarrassing reaction may be far less exclusive than your brain claims.
rituals.predict: Guess what percentage of ordinary people would have some version of the same reaction.
rituals.play: Imagine ten people in the same situation. Give at least three of them plausible internal reactions similar to yours, even if they hide them differently.
rituals.catch: Check if the feeling becomes less like evidence of personal defect.
rituals.reveal: We often underestimate how common our uncomfortable traits and reactions are.
rituals.mindBend: Private weirdness is often public humanity with better camouflage.

rituals.name: REVERSE THE CONDITIONAL
rituals.title: REVERSE THE CONDITIONAL
rituals.targetPattern: Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)
rituals.target_pattern: Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)
rituals.precise_subpattern: Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A)
rituals.vibeLine: Same words, reversed logic, completely different claim.
rituals.hook: Your brain flipped the direction of the evidence without asking.
rituals.predict: Guess whether 'most anxious people notice symptoms' means 'most people who notice symptoms are anxious.'
rituals.play: Write the claim as A GIVEN B. Reverse it to B GIVEN A. Ask whether the reversed statement has been shown.
rituals.catch: Notice how easy it is for the two directions to feel identical.
rituals.reveal: Conditional probabilities change when you reverse them.
rituals.mindBend: Evidence can point one way without pointing equally hard back.

VIBE: JOLLY

Probability arrow has been caught doing a U-turn.

HOOK
Your brain flipped the direction of the evidence without asking.

PREDICT
Guess whether 'most anxious people notice symptoms' means 'most people who notice symptoms are anxious.'

PLAY
Write the claim as A GIVEN B. Reverse it to B GIVEN A. Ask whether the reversed statement has been shown.

CATCH
Notice how easy it is for the two directions to feel identical.

REVEAL
Conditional probabilities change when you reverse them.

MIND BEND
Evidence can point one way without pointing equally hard back.

MOVE ON
↻ REVERSE THE CONDITIONAL

rituals.precise_subpattern: Rare evidence mistaken for rare innocence
rituals.vibeLine: Very dramatic clue. Still not the whole case.
rituals.hook: A rare clue sounds powerful until you ask how many innocent cases could also produce it.
rituals.predict: Guess how many non-target situations could generate the same evidence.
rituals.play: Take one striking clue. List three innocent or ordinary pathways that could also create it.
rituals.catch: Check if the clue still feels like a verdict.
rituals.reveal: Rare evidence is not identical to low probability of innocence.

rituals.vibeLine: Existing choice was pretending to be empty space.
rituals.hook: The current setup is wearing a disguise called 'nothing.'
rituals.predict: Guess what costs you pay by staying exactly as you are.

rituals.catch: Notice how status quo stops looking free.
rituals.reveal: Existing arrangements feel neutral because their costs are familiar.
rituals.mindBend: Doing what you already do is still a decision with a price.

rituals.title: THE PIE MIGHT GROW
rituals.targetPattern: Assuming another person's gain must reduce one's own outcome
rituals.target_pattern: Assuming another person's gain must reduce one's own outcome
rituals.precise_subpattern: Assuming another person's gain must reduce one's own outcome
rituals.vibeLine: Their slice may not have come off your plate.
rituals.hook: Your brain saw someone else gain and quietly shrank your slice.
rituals.predict: Guess what exactly you lose if they gain.
rituals.play: Take the comparison. Name the resource: money, attention, opportunity, praise, love, status. Ask whether it is truly fixed, partly expandable, or unrelated.
rituals.catch: Notice if the loss was assumed before the resource was defined.
rituals.reveal: Not every social resource is a fixed pie.
rituals.mindBend: Someone else's gain can be real without being your subtraction.

rituals.name: YESTERDAY ISN'T EVIDENCE ENOUGH
rituals.title: YESTERDAY ISN'T EVIDENCE ENOUGH
rituals.targetPattern: Assuming tomorrow will resemble yesterday despite credible change signals
rituals.target_pattern: Assuming tomorrow will resemble yesterday despite credible change signals
rituals.precise_subpattern: Assuming tomorrow will resemble yesterday despite credible change signals
rituals.vibeLine: Usually fine is not a force field.
rituals.hook: Familiarity can make change signals feel less real than they are.
rituals.predict: Guess which fact you are discounting mainly because 'it usually works out.'
rituals.play: List one reason things may stay normal and one concrete new signal that says conditions changed. Give both equal sentence length.
rituals.catch: Check if habit had been carrying more weight than evidence.
rituals.reveal: People can underreact to credible change because normality feels safer and more probable.
rituals.mindBend: A long ordinary past does not cancel new information.

rituals.precise_subpattern: Accepting a system recommendation without independently checking an obvious cue
rituals.vibeLine: Useful machine, still not emperor.
rituals.hook: A confident system output can make your own eyes go strangely quiet.
rituals.predict: Guess what evidence you would check if the recommendation came from a random stranger instead.
rituals.play: Take a harmless automated suggestion—route, spellcheck, recommendation, score. Name one independent cue you can verify before accepting it.
rituals.catch: Notice how authority shifted when the source became a system.
rituals.reveal: Automation can reduce vigilance even when human judgment still matters.
rituals.mindBend: A machine can be useful without becoming the only witness.

rituals.precise_subpattern: Failing to notice a choice has been switched and then explaining the switched option
rituals.vibeLine: Great reasons. Wrong original choice.
rituals.hook: Your brain is frighteningly good at explaining choices—even choices it did not make.

rituals.catch: Notice how explanation ability is not proof of original preference.
rituals.reveal: People can construct reasons after the fact for choices they did not actually make.
rituals.mindBend: A convincing explanation can be generated after the decision, not discovered before it.

rituals.title: MORE PIECES FEELS LIKE MORE
rituals.targetPattern: More separate pieces feeling like more total amount even when quantity is equal
rituals.target_pattern: More separate pieces feeling like more total amount even when quantity is equal
rituals.precise_subpattern: More separate pieces feeling like more total amount even when quantity is equal
rituals.vibeLine: Twenty pieces brought more visual drama than five.
rituals.hook: Your brain can confuse number of pieces with total amount.
rituals.predict: Guess which feels like more: twenty tiny coins or five larger coins worth the same total.
rituals.play: Take an equal total represented as many small units versus a few large units—money, tasks, snacks, files. Compare intuitive amount before calculating.
rituals.catch: Check if 'more pieces' quietly became 'more total.'
rituals.reveal: Numerosity is a salient shortcut for magnitude.
rituals.mindBend: More things is not always more amount.

rituals.name: EXPLAIN THE GEARS
rituals.title: EXPLAIN THE GEARS
rituals.targetPattern: Feeling one understands something until asked to explain the mechanism step by step
rituals.target_pattern: Feeling one understands something until asked to explain the mechanism step by step
rituals.precise_subpattern: Feeling one understands something until asked to explain the mechanism step by step
rituals.vibeLine: You knew the noun. The gears were on annual leave.
rituals.hook: Knowing the label can feel suspiciously like knowing how the thing works.
rituals.predict: Guess how many steps you can explain without using the name of the thing as the explanation.
rituals.play: Choose something ordinary you feel you understand—zipper, toilet, inflation, Wi-Fi. Explain the mechanism in five concrete steps.
rituals.catch: Catch the exact step where explanation turns into hand-waving.
rituals.reveal: People routinely overestimate the depth of their causal understanding.
rituals.mindBend: Familiarity with a thing is not the same as a working model of it.

rituals.title: PAPER ODDS VS LIVED SAMPLE
rituals.targetPattern: Choices changing when probabilities are learned from lived samples rather than stated numbers
rituals.target_pattern: Choices changing when probabilities are learned from lived samples rather than stated numbers
rituals.precise_subpattern: Choices changing when probabilities are learned from lived samples rather than stated numbers
rituals.vibeLine: Probability and personal sample are not the same department.
rituals.hook: A probability on paper and a probability you meet in ten experiences can feel like different worlds.
rituals.predict: Guess how risky a 10% event feels after seeing it happen zero times in your last ten experiences.
rituals.play: Compare two versions: '10% chance' written down, versus ten imagined trials where none happens. Imagine one happens first.
rituals.catch: Notice how recent experience pulls intuition away from the stated rate.
rituals.reveal: Rare outcomes are weighted differently when learned through description versus sampling.
rituals.mindBend: Your lived sample can feel more convincing than the true probability—even when it is tiny.

rituals.name: CONFIDENCE CHANGES WITH DIFFICULTY
rituals.title: CONFIDENCE CHANGES WITH DIFFICULTY
rituals.targetPattern: Confidence miscalibrating differently on easy versus difficult questions
rituals.target_pattern: Confidence miscalibrating differently on easy versus difficult questions
rituals.precise_subpattern: Confidence miscalibrating differently on easy versus difficult questions
rituals.vibeLine: Same brain, different swagger depending on question difficulty.
rituals.hook: Your confidence meter may be badly calibrated at both ends.
rituals.predict: Guess whether you tend to understate easy answers and overstate hard guesses.
rituals.play: Pick five easy factual questions and five difficult ones. Give an answer and confidence percentage before checking.
rituals.catch: Check if calibration error changes with difficulty.
rituals.reveal: People often show underconfidence on easy items and overconfidence on difficult ones.
rituals.mindBend: Confidence is not one fixed skill; it can bend with task difficulty.

VIBE: UNFILTERED

Do not trust one damn confidence habit across every damn terrain.

HOOK
Your confidence meter may be badly calibrated at both ends.

PREDICT
Guess whether you tend to understate easy answers and overstate hard guesses.

PLAY
Pick five easy factual questions and five difficult ones. Give an answer and confidence percentage before checking.

CATCH
Check if calibration error changes with difficulty.

REVEAL
People often show underconfidence on easy items and overconfidence on difficult ones.

MIND BEND
Confidence is not one fixed skill; it can bend with task difficulty.

MOVE ON
↻ CONFIDENCE CHANGES WITH DIFFICULTY

rituals.title: COMPOUNDING ISN'T A STRAIGHT LINE
rituals.targetPattern: Compounding change intuitively underestimated because the mind expects linear growth
rituals.target_pattern: Compounding change intuitively underestimated because the mind expects linear growth
rituals.precise_subpattern: Compounding change intuitively underestimated because the mind expects linear growth
rituals.vibeLine: Compounding starts boring and ends rude.
rituals.hook: Your brain draws a straight line through a curve.
rituals.predict: Guess which grows more: adding 10 each round or increasing by 10% each round over many rounds.
rituals.play: Write the first five steps of both sequences. Continue two more than feels necessary.
rituals.catch: Catch the point where the compounding path starts surprising you.
rituals.reveal: People systematically underestimate exponential growth.
rituals.mindBend: A slow curve can outrun a fast-looking straight line.

People overweight introspection when explaining themselves and observable behaviour when explaining others.

Your private reasons matter, but your behaviour is evidence too.

rituals.title: CERTAINTY FLIPS THE PICK
rituals.targetPattern: Preference changing when identical probability mass is added to both risky options
rituals.target_pattern: Preference changing when identical probability mass is added to both risky options
rituals.precise_subpattern: Preference changing when identical probability mass is added to both risky options
rituals.vibeLine: Same contest, new probability costume, different winner.
rituals.hook: Two choices can preserve the same payoff difference and still flip your preference.
rituals.predict: Guess whether adding the same extra chance of getting nothing to both options should change which option you prefer.
rituals.play: Compare: A = guaranteed $30; B = 80% chance $40. Imagine both receive the same additional 75% chance of nothing, leaving only scaled-down winning chances. Recheck preference.
rituals.catch: Check if the common change alters your appetite for certainty.
rituals.reveal: Preferences under risk can violate simple consistency when certainty is introduced or removed.
rituals.mindBend: The difference between options can stay structurally similar while certainty changes the feeling of the choice.

rituals.precise_subpattern: A bad outcome creating an urge to invent a deservingness explanation
rituals.vibeLine: Terrible outcome, not necessarily a character review.
rituals.hook: When something unfair happens, the brain can try to make the world feel orderly by blaming the person.
rituals.predict: Guess whether you would search harder for 'what they did wrong' after hearing the bad outcome first.
rituals.play: Take a harmless unlucky outcome. List one behavioural cause, one situational cause, and one chance cause before judging deservingness.
rituals.catch: Check if moral explanation was appearing faster than causal evidence.
rituals.reveal: Belief in a just world can make random or structural misfortune feel as if it must have been deserved.
rituals.mindBend: A fair world is comforting; inventing guilt does not make it fair.

unfiltered.displayName: ONE PERCENT HAS A LOUD VOICE
unfiltered.openingLine:
Do not let damn possibility shout louder than the damn probability.

Going from zero chance to tiny chance can feel much bigger than the maths says.
unfiltered.ritualCard:
Going from zero chance to tiny chance can feel much bigger than the maths says.
Write both as identical one-percentage-point changes. Notice which one changes your emotion more.
Guess which change feels larger: 0%→1% or 40%→41%.
Catch 'possible at all' acting like a special category. Very small probabilities can be overweighted because possibility itself is psychologically salient.

rituals.name: THREE SOURCES OR ONE ECHO?
rituals.title: THREE SOURCES OR ONE ECHO?
rituals.targetPattern: Multiple correlated pieces of evidence feeling like multiple independent confirmations
rituals.target_pattern: Multiple correlated pieces of evidence feeling like multiple independent confirmations
rituals.precise_subpattern: Multiple correlated pieces of evidence feeling like multiple independent confirmations
rituals.vibeLine: Echo chamber submitted duplicate receipts.
rituals.hook: Three articles can feel like three confirmations even when they all copied the same source.
rituals.predict: Guess how many independent evidence chains sit behind the claims you saw.
rituals.play: Trace each piece one step backward: original data, press release, same expert, same study, same rumour. Group echoes together.
rituals.catch: Notice the evidence pile shrink when dependencies appear.
rituals.reveal: Correlated reports provide less independent evidence than their count suggests.
rituals.mindBend: Repetition across channels is not the same as independent confirmation.
